error_modes.label: Altitude control on the vectors until established on final

texts.0: SP, due to a pitch change made for the turn onto the downwind vector without a matching power correction, did not maintain the altitude assigned by the controller before final descent. The aircraft went more than 300 feet low with the deviation still increasing, and the IP took the aircraft to re-establish the assigned level. SP did not reference the altimeter or the VVI at any point during the vectoring turns.
texts.1: SP, due to a trim setting left unchanged after the configuration change on the base leg, did not hold the assigned altitude during the vectors to final. Deviation reached the 300 foot limit of the standard and was reduced only after the controller and then the IP verbally prompted a check of the altitude. The aircraft was returned to the assigned level shortly before intercepting final.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held on the heading bug during each controller-issued turn, did not keep the pitch and power combination that held the assigned altitude. Deviation opened to about 230 feet, between the 150 and 300 foot values of the standard, before SP detected the trend on the altimeter and recovered the assigned level without IP input. The remaining vectors were flown on altitude.
texts.3: SP maintained every altitude assigned by the controller during the vectors to final within 150 feet. Level-offs were anticipated with a lead point and the altitude was held through each turn without a power correction being needed late. Deviations that appeared were removed as soon as they showed on the altimeter.
texts.4: SP held the assigned altitudes on the vectors to final essentially exactly, with excursions no greater than about 40 feet through the turns and configuration changes. Each level-off was anticipated and required no correction after roll-out. The altimeter needle stayed effectively motionless while the heading changes were flown.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the assigned altitudes within the published tolerance, but the deviation sat near the 150 foot edge of the standard for most of the vectoring phase rather than being held closer to the assigned level. Corrections were applied in single late steps at the end of each turn. SP is expected to anticipate the pitch and power change at the start of each turn so the altitude error stays well inside the standard.

texts.0: SP, due to roll-outs flown without a computed lead point on the assigned heading, did not fly the headings issued by the controller during the ASR approach. Heading error exceeded 10 degrees on final with no correction started, the controller repeated the correction twice, and the IP intervened to place the aircraft back on the assigned heading. SP did not use the HSI to detect the drift off the issued heading between corrections.
texts.1: SP, due to corrections applied in bank angles too large for the small heading changes issued on final, did not settle on the assigned headings. Heading error reached the 10 degree limit of the standard on each correction and was contained only after repeated controller calls and a verbal prompt from the IP. The aircraft was oscillating either side of the assigned heading through most of final.
texts.2: SP, due to a delay in starting each turn after the controller issued the new heading, did not track the assigned heading continuously. Error reached about 8 degrees, between the 5 and 10 degree values of the standard, before SP recognized it on the HSI and rolled out on the assigned heading without IP input. The subsequent corrections were taken up promptly.
texts.3: SP flew every heading issued by the controller and held it within 5 degrees throughout the approach. Turns were started immediately on receipt of the correction and rolled out on the assigned value with a suitable lead. No repeat of a heading instruction was required.
texts.4: SP took up each controller-issued heading at once and held it to within about 2 degrees for the whole of final. Corrections were made in small, damped bank inputs that produced no overshoot on roll-out. The controller issued no repeat and no correcting call for azimuth.
texts.marginal: SP flew the assigned headings within the published tolerance, but the error tended toward the 5 degree edge of the standard between corrections and the aircraft wandered slowly off each new heading once established. The trend was arrested only when the controller issued the next instruction. SP is expected to hold the assigned heading actively against drift rather than relying on the next controller call.

error_modes.label: Airspeed control on the ASR final

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate monitoring of airspeed during the approach, did not maintain the computed final approach airspeed after the descent was started. Airspeed decayed more than 10 knots below the computed value with no power correction applied, and the IP added power and took the aircraft. SP did not identify the decay from the airspeed indicator before the intervention.
texts.1: SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check while attention stayed on the controller's azimuth calls, did not correct the airspeed as the aircraft descended. Airspeed reached 20 knots above the computed value at the 10 knot limit on the slow side of the following correction, and was contained only after the IP prompted a power check. The approach was flown to MDA with the airspeed still oscillating.
texts.2: SP, due to a cross-check interval that lengthened each time the controller transmitted, did not hold a stable power setting on final. Airspeed drifted to about 15 knots above the computed value, between the plus 10 and plus 20 knot values of the standard, before SP saw it on the airspeed indicator and reduced power to recover it without IP input. The remainder of final was flown on speed.
texts.3: SP maintained the computed final approach airspeed within 10 knots fast and 5 knots slow throughout the ASR final. Power was set for the descent and adjusted in small increments as the configuration and the descent rate changed. The airspeed indicator was included in the cross-check between every controller transmission.
texts.4: SP held the computed final approach airspeed to within about 3 knots for the whole of final, including through the descent and the configuration change. Power corrections were small and anticipatory, and no speed excursion of consequence developed. The airspeed remained stable while every controller call was answered.
texts.marginal: SP kept the airspeed within the published tolerance, but it sat close to the 10 knot fast edge of the standard for much of final and was brought back only when the descent rate had to be re-established. Power corrections were reactive rather than anticipatory. SP is expected to shorten the interval between airspeed checks so the speed is held nearer the computed value.

error_modes.label: Altitude control at MDA and the no-descent-below limit

texts.0: SP, due to a descent rate carried into the level-off without a lead point, did not stop the descent at the published MDA. The aircraft went below MDA on an approach where no descent below that altitude is permitted, and the IP arrested the descent and levelled the aircraft. SP did not recognize the penetration of MDA from the altimeter until the intervention.
texts.1: SP, due to a late reduction of the descent rate as MDA was approached, did not level off close to the published minimum. The aircraft stopped 200 feet above MDA at the limit of the standard and was brought down to the correct level-off only after the IP prompted a check of the altitude against the approach plate. The level segment to the missed approach point was flown high.
texts.2: SP, due to a level-off started without reference to the descent rate then being flown, did not capture MDA closely. Level-off occurred about 160 feet above MDA, between the plus 100 and plus 200 foot values of the standard, before SP recognized the excess altitude and descended to the correct minimum without IP input, with no descent below MDA at any point. The level segment was then held accurately.
texts.3: SP levelled off at the published MDA within 100 feet above it and at no point descended below the minimum. The level-off was anticipated from the descent rate and the altitude was then held to the missed approach point. The altimeter setting and the published minimum were confirmed before the descent was started.
texts.4: SP captured MDA within about 30 feet above the published minimum and held it precisely to the missed approach point, with no descent below MDA. The level-off required no correction after the initial power and pitch change. The minimum was flown as briefed and confirmed against the approach plate before the final descent.
texts.marginal: SP levelled off within the published tolerance above MDA and did not descend below it, but the capture was about 90 feet high, close to the edge of the standard, and the aircraft settled onto the minimum only part way along the level segment. The lead point for the level-off was short for the descent rate flown. SP is expected to set the lead point from the actual descent rate so MDA is captured closer to the published minimum.

error_modes.label: Compliance with and read-back of controller instructions

texts.0: SP, due to an unstandard read-back that did not confirm the actual clearance, did not comply with the instructions issued by the approach controller. A heading and a descent clearance were both actioned incorrectly, the controller queried the aircraft twice, and the IP took over the radios and the aircraft to re-establish the approach. SP did not request a repeat of the instruction that had not been understood.
texts.1: SP, due to non-standard phraseology that left the intention ambiguous to the controller, did not comply promptly with the instructions given on the ASR. Two instructions had to be repeated by the controller before they were flown, and compliance came only after the IP prompted the response, with the resulting heading error at the 10 degree limit of the standard. The approach was completed with the controller leading the aircraft rather than the aircraft following the vectors.
texts.2: SP, due to a read-back given before the instruction had been fully received, did not action one controller instruction at the moment it was issued. The delay produced a deviation of about 8 degrees in azimuth, between the 5 and 10 degree values of the standard, which SP corrected without IP input after re-confirming the assigned heading with the controller. The remaining instructions were read back correctly and flown immediately.
texts.3: SP read back every controller instruction in standard phraseology and complied with it without delay. Headings, descent clearances and the approach sequence were actioned as issued, and no instruction required repetition. Radio work did not displace control of the flown parameters.
texts.4: SP handled the approach frequency in standard phraseology throughout, read back each instruction accurately and flew it immediately, with no query from the controller at any stage. Transmissions were short and timed so they did not interrupt the instrument cross-check. The controller was able to run the ASR without a single repeat.
texts.marginal: SP complied with all controller instructions and remained within the published tolerances, but several read-backs used non-standard wording and compliance followed the instruction by a noticeable pause. No deviation reached the edge of a standard, though the pattern of late responses left little margin on final. SP is expected to use standard phraseology and to begin the correction as the read-back is made.

error_modes.label: Observance of published routing and altitude restrictions

texts.0: SP, due to an approach flown without reference to the published minimum altitudes for the segment, did not observe the routing and altitude restrictions of the MAIP and the approach manual. The aircraft was flown more than 300 feet below the published segment minimum while still being vectored, and the IP intervened to climb back to a safe altitude. SP did not compare the assigned altitude with the published restriction at any point.
texts.1: SP, due to a descent started on the controller's advisory before the aircraft was inside the segment where it was published, did not respect the applicable altitude restriction. The aircraft reached the 300 foot limit of the standard below the published segment altitude and was returned to it only after the IP called the restriction. The remainder of the approach was flown with the plate held rather than briefed.
texts.2: SP, due to a briefing of the approach that covered the final segment but not the intermediate restrictions, did not apply one published altitude limit at the correct point. The aircraft was about 230 feet low against the segment minimum, between the 150 and 300 foot values of the standard, before SP identified the restriction on the plate and climbed back without IP input. No further restriction was missed.
texts.3: SP flew the ASR within the routing and altitude restrictions published in the MAIP and the approach manual. The applicable segment minima were known from the approach briefing and each descent was started only where it was authorized. No restriction had to be recalled by the controller or the IP.
texts.4: SP observed every published routing and altitude restriction precisely, with the aircraft never closer than a comfortable margin to a segment minimum before the point at which descent was authorized. The approach plate had been briefed in full and the applicable limits were quoted from memory when queried. The vectors were flown entirely within the published protected area.
texts.marginal: SP remained within the published routing and altitude restrictions, but the aircraft was flown close to a segment minimum with the descent started at the earliest point rather than with a working margin. No restriction was violated and no deviation approached the edge of a standard. SP is expected to build a margin against the published minima instead of flying the approach at the limit of what is authorized.

error_modes.label: Sequence, checklist and configuration timing on the approach

texts.0: SP, due to workload management that left the checklist unfinished before the descent, did not execute the approach sequence as described in the flight manual and AFMAN 11-202 Vol 3. The aircraft was still unconfigured when the descent to MDA was started, airspeed went more than 10 knots below the computed value, and the IP configured the aircraft and took control. SP did not run the before landing items at any point on the approach.
texts.1: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated all cockpit work inside the turn to final, did not complete the required actions in the order and at the points prescribed. The configuration change was made after the descent had begun and the resulting speed excursion reached the 20 knot fast limit of the standard, contained only after the IP prompted the checklist. The approach was completed with the sequence recovered but never fully caught up.
texts.2: SP, due to a checklist started later than the briefed point, did not complete the configuration before the final descent was due. Airspeed rose to about 15 knots above the computed value, between the plus 10 and plus 20 knot values of the standard, while the items were completed, and SP restored the correct speed and sequence without IP input. The remaining approach items were run at the briefed points.
texts.3: SP executed the approach in the sequence prescribed by the flight manual and the published procedure. Checklists were completed at the briefed points, the aircraft was configured before the descent was started, and the flown parameters stayed inside the standards while the items were run. No item required prompting.
texts.4: SP ran the approach sequence exactly as briefed, with each checklist completed ahead of the point at which it was required and the configuration established well before the descent. Cockpit work was distributed so that no phase of the approach carried a peak of tasks, and the flown parameters were unaffected throughout. The whole approach was completed without a single reminder.
texts.marginal: SP completed the approach sequence and all required checklist items, but several were run at the latest usable point and the workload was concentrated in the turn to final. The parameters stayed inside the standards, though the margin narrowed each time an item was completed late. SP is expected to move the checklist and configuration actions forward so the workload is spread across the approach.

error_modes.label: Instrument cross-check while flying controller-directed azimuth

texts.0: SP, due to a scan that stopped on the HSI each time the controller transmitted, did not maintain the instrument cross-check required to fly the ASR without mistakes. Attitude, altitude and airspeed all went unmonitored, the altitude deviation passed 300 feet, and the IP took the aircraft. SP was unable to state the aircraft state when asked during the approach.
texts.1: SP, due to a cross-check that reduced to the attitude indicator and the heading during the controller's corrections, did not detect the developing deviations on the supporting instruments. Altitude error reached the 300 foot limit of the standard before it was noticed, and the scan was restored only after the IP verbally directed attention to the altimeter. The pattern repeated on the second half of final.
texts.2: SP, due to a cross-check interrupted at each controller call and restarted from the same instrument, did not sample the altimeter and the airspeed indicator often enough. Altitude drifted to about 230 feet, between the 150 and 300 foot values of the standard, before SP re-established the full scan and recovered the assigned altitude without IP input. The scan pattern was then maintained to MDA.
texts.3: SP maintained a continuous instrument cross-check through the vectoring and the final descent, sampling attitude, heading, altitude and airspeed in a regular pattern. Each controller transmission was answered without the scan being suspended, and every deviation was detected while it was still small. All flown parameters stayed inside the standards.
texts.4: SP kept a complete and evenly paced instrument cross-check throughout the ASR, with no instrument left unsampled through the turns, the descent and the level-off at MDA. Deviations were detected and removed before they became measurable, and the radio work never displaced the scan. SP was able to report the full aircraft state at any point on request.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the instrument cross-check and stayed inside the published tolerances, but the scan narrowed toward the heading indication whenever the controller transmitted and the altimeter was sampled at longer intervals than the rest. Deviations were caught, though later than the scan should allow. SP is expected to keep the sampling rate of the altimeter and the airspeed indicator constant through the controller's calls.

error_modes.label: Missed approach decision and execution at the missed approach point

texts.0: SP, due to a missed approach procedure that had not been briefed before the approach was started, did not execute the published missed approach at the missed approach point. The aircraft was held at MDA past the missed approach point with no climb and no turn initiated, and the IP took the aircraft to fly the published procedure. SP did not identify the missed approach point from the controller's advisories or the timing.
texts.1: SP, due to a decision deferred while the runway environment was still being sought, did not start the missed approach at the published point. The climb was begun late and the aircraft drifted to the 10 degree limit of the standard off the published missed approach heading, corrected only after the IP prompted the procedure. The initial climb was flown without the configuration being fully cleaned up.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow transition from the level segment to the climb, did not initiate the missed approach as promptly as the procedure requires. Heading error on the initial climb-out reached about 8 degrees, between the 5 and 10 degree values of the standard, before SP recognized it and re-established the published track without IP input. The configuration change and the climb were then completed correctly.
texts.3: SP initiated the published missed approach at the missed approach point without delay, established the climb and flew the published track. The procedure had been briefed before the approach and the aircraft was cleaned up in the correct sequence while the climb was maintained. Heading and airspeed stayed inside the standards throughout the transition.
texts.4: SP flew the missed approach exactly at the published point, with power, attitude and configuration applied in the correct order and the published track held from the start of the climb. The intention was passed to the controller in standard phraseology as the climb began. No parameter departed from the standard during the transition.
texts.marginal: SP executed the published missed approach at the correct point and within the tolerances, but the climb was established a few seconds after the point was reached and the initial track was regained rather than flown from the start. The procedure was correct in content and slightly late in timing. SP is expected to pre-set the missed approach decision so the climb begins as the point is reached.

error_modes.label: Overcontrolling heading with corrections larger than 5 degrees

texts.0: SP, due to course corrections taken with heading changes far larger than the 5 degree limit of the technique, did not damp the azimuth corrections passed by the controller. Every correction was followed by an overshoot in the opposite direction, heading error passed 10 degrees with the oscillation still growing, and the IP took the aircraft to steady the final. SP made no attempt to keep the corrections inside the area beneath the heading bug.
texts.1: SP, due to heading corrections applied well outside the area beneath the heading bug, did not stop the tendency to overcorrect once the controller began passing azimuth calls. Heading error reached about 10 degrees, at the limit of the standard, on two successive corrections and came down only after the IP called for the corrections to be halved. The oscillation about the final course continued to the missed approach point.
texts.2: SP, due to corrections that exceeded the 5 degree limit each time the controller called a heading change, did not settle the aircraft on the final course at the first attempt. The overshoot reached about 8 degrees, between the 5 and 10 degree values of the standard, before SP reduced the size of the inputs and steadied the heading without IP input. The later calls were flown with small corrections.
texts.3: SP kept the azimuth corrections at or below the 5 degree limit of the technique, so only small overshoots appeared on roll-out. Heading error stayed within about 4 degrees of the assigned heading, inside the standard, and each correction was damped on the following one. The final course was regained without an oscillation developing.
texts.4: SP made every azimuth correction inside the width of the heading bug, so no correction produced an overshoot. Heading error remained of the order of 1 to 2 degrees and the aircraft followed the controller's azimuth calls smoothly. The controller reported the aircraft on course for the whole of final.
texts.marginal: SP kept the heading errors within the published tolerance, but corrections were consistently taken at more than 5 degrees and each was followed by an overshoot that reached the 5 degree edge of the standard. The oscillation was contained but never fully damped. SP is expected to limit heading changes to the area beneath the heading bug so a correction stops the deviation instead of reversing it.

error_modes.label: Heading bug not marked with the wind corrected final approach heading

texts.0: SP, due to the heading bug being left on the last vector instead of being marked with the wind corrected heading for the final, did not have the additional visual cue of heading deviations that the technique provides. The aircraft drifted more than 10 degrees off the final approach heading with no correction started, and the IP set the bug and took the aircraft back onto the course. SP had not produced a wind corrected heading before the approach.
texts.1: SP, due to a heading bug left unset for the final approach course, worked the azimuth calls from the raw heading indication alone. Heading error reached about 10 degrees, at the limit of the standard, and steadied only after the IP called for the bug to be set on the final approach heading. The rest of the approach needed repeated verbal cues on azimuth.
texts.2: SP, due to the heading bug being marked only after the turn to final was complete, had no visual reference for the wind corrected heading when the drift first appeared. The error grew to about 7 degrees, between the 5 and 10 degree values of the standard, before SP set the bug and returned the aircraft to the final approach heading without IP input.
texts.3: SP set the heading bug to the wind corrected final approach heading before the turn onto final and used it as the reference for the azimuth calls. Deviations stayed within about 4 degrees of the bugged heading, inside the standard, and were seen as soon as the indication moved off the bug. Corrections were kept beneath the bug.
texts.4: SP marked the wind corrected heading on the bug during the vectors and flew the whole final against it, with the heading indication effectively pinned to the bug. Any drift was detected the moment it appeared and removed with a correction of a degree or two. The controller passed no azimuth correction.
texts.marginal: SP flew against a heading bug set for the final, but the bugged value was the published course with no allowance for the wind, so the aircraft sat near the 5 degree edge of the standard on one side for much of final. The deviation was contained by repeated small corrections rather than removed at its source. SP is expected to bug the wind corrected heading so the bug shows real deviations rather than a constant offset.

error_modes.label: Drift correction not calculated from the winds or from GPS track

texts.0: SP, due to a drift correction that was never calculated with the 60 to 1 rule and no comparison of GPS track against aircraft heading, did not establish a wind corrected heading for the ASR final. The aircraft was carried steadily off the final course until the heading error exceeded 10 degrees with no correction started, and the IP took the aircraft after the controller reported the aircraft well off centerline. SP could not state the crosswind component when asked.
texts.1: SP, due to the crosswind component never being divided by the airspeed in NM per minute to produce a drift figure, flew the final on the published course heading. The aircraft drifted until the required correction reached about 10 degrees, at the limit of the standard, and a wind corrected heading was taken up only after the IP prompted the calculation.
texts.2: SP, due to a drift allowance judged by eye rather than computed from the winds or read from the GPS, did not hold a heading that stopped the drift off the final course. Azimuth error grew to about 8 degrees, between the 5 and 10 degree values of the standard, before SP compared track with heading on the GPS, took up a corrected heading and stopped the drift without IP input.
texts.3: SP computed the drift from the known winds with the 60 to 1 rule and flew the resulting wind corrected heading down the final. Residual azimuth error stayed within about 4 degrees, inside the standard, and was removed with single small corrections. Track was compared with heading on the GPS once on final to confirm the figure.
texts.4: SP calculated the drift before the approach and refined it by comparing GPS track with heading during the vectors, so the final was flown on a heading that held the course with no measurable drift. Corrections were of the order of a degree and the controller reported the aircraft on centerline throughout.
texts.marginal: SP applied a drift correction, but the figure was rounded rather than derived from the crosswind component, so the aircraft crept toward the 5 degree edge of the standard on one side of the final course. The deviation was reset by repeated corrections while the drift itself remained. SP is expected to calculate the drift with the 60 to 1 rule so the heading holds the course without repeated resets.

error_modes.label: Pitch corrections larger than 2 degrees during the descent to MDA

texts.0: SP, due to pitch corrections far larger than the 2 degree limit of the technique, chased the descent rate with alternating large inputs on the way to MDA. The VSI swung well beyond the 400 feet per minute that 2 degrees of pitch represents, the aircraft went below MDA on an approach where no descent below the minimum is permitted, and the IP arrested the descent and took the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to pitch changes of several degrees applied each time the descent rate was checked, did not settle the aircraft on a steady rate to the minimum. The oscillation left the level-off about 200 feet above MDA, at the limit of the standard, and the aircraft was brought onto the minimum only after repeated IP calls on rate and altitude.
texts.2: SP, due to pitch corrections that exceeded 2 degrees and produced VSI swings well past 400 feet per minute, did not hold the descent rate that would place the aircraft at MDA. Level-off occurred about 160 feet above MDA, between the plus 100 and plus 200 foot values of the standard, before SP reduced the size of the pitch inputs and settled onto the minimum without IP input.
texts.3: SP kept pitch corrections at or below 2 degrees on the descent, so the VSI moved in steps of about 400 feet per minute and the rate stayed close to the value required. Level-off was inside 100 feet above MDA, within the standard, with no descent below the minimum. The altitude was then held steady to the missed approach point.
texts.4: SP flew the descent with pitch corrections of a degree or less and the rate stayed effectively constant to the minimum. The aircraft levelled about 25 feet above MDA with no descent below it and needed no correction after the level-off. The VSI showed no oscillation at any point on final.
texts.marginal: SP kept the level-off inside the published tolerance, but the descent was flown with pitch inputs larger than 2 degrees and the VSI oscillated about the required rate, so the capture finished around 90 feet above MDA at the edge of the standard. No descent below the minimum occurred. SP is expected to limit pitch changes to 2 degrees so the rate stays stable and MDA is captured close to the minimum.

error_modes.label: Large power corrections instead of small changes on final

texts.0: SP, due to large power corrections applied instead of the small changes the technique calls for, did not hold the 110 KIAS final approach airspeed. Each correction was reversed by a larger one, airspeed fell more than 10 knots below the approach speed with torque still being moved through wide ranges, and the IP set the power and took the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to power moved in large steps whenever the airspeed indication changed, did not stabilize the speed on final. Airspeed reached about 20 knots above the approach speed, at the limit of the standard, and was contained only after the IP called for a fixed torque setting with small trims from it.
texts.2: SP, due to power corrections much larger than the speed error present required, did not settle on the torque setting for the configured final. Airspeed swung to about 15 knots above 110 KIAS, between the plus 10 and plus 20 knot values of the standard, before SP reduced the size of the power changes and recovered the approach speed without IP input.
texts.3: SP made small power corrections around the torque setting for the configured final and held the airspeed inside the standard, no more than about 8 knots fast and 4 knots slow of 110 KIAS. No correction had to be reversed, and each speed trend was stopped rather than overshot.
texts.4: SP held 110 KIAS to within about 3 knots for the whole of final on an essentially fixed torque setting, with only trimming changes of a percent or two. Large power corrections were never needed because no speed error was allowed to build. The configuration change was absorbed without an excursion.
texts.marginal: SP stayed within the published airspeed tolerance, but the speed was held by a series of oversized power corrections that carried it from one side of the approach speed to the other and touched the 10 knot fast edge of the standard. The aircraft never settled on a steady torque setting. SP is expected to avoid large power corrections unless the airspeed is excessively high or low and to trim from a known setting instead.

error_modes.label: Configuration completed later than 2 to 3 NM prior to the FAF

texts.0: SP, due to the aircraft being configured well inside the 2 to 3 NM point before the FAF, did not have airspeed and trim stabilized when the descent was due. Gear and flap changes were still taking effect as the descent began, airspeed went more than 10 knots below the approach speed with the aircraft out of trim, and the IP took the aircraft and re-established a stabilized final.
texts.1: SP, due to configuration started at the FAF rather than 2 to 3 NM before it, began the descent with the trim still being chased. Airspeed rose to about 20 knots above the approach speed, at the limit of the standard, while the trim was set, and the speed was recovered only under IP direction on power and trim.
texts.2: SP, due to gear and flaps being selected later than the 2 to 3 NM point, had no time to stabilize airspeed and trim before descending at the FAF. Airspeed moved to about 14 knots above 110 KIAS, between the plus 10 and plus 20 knot values of the standard, while the trim change was absorbed, and SP recovered the approach speed without IP input.
texts.3: SP configured the aircraft close to the 2 to 3 NM point before the FAF, so airspeed and trim were essentially settled when the descent began. Speed stayed inside the standard, no more than about 8 knots fast and 4 knots slow of 110 KIAS, through the configuration change and the start of the descent.
texts.4: SP had gear down, flaps TO and the Before-Landing Checklist complete well before the 2 to 3 NM point and the aircraft trimmed for 110 KIAS ahead of the FAF. The descent was started from a fully stabilized state and airspeed varied by no more than about 3 knots. No trim input was needed once the descent began.
texts.marginal: SP configured just inside the 2 to 3 NM point and reached the FAF with the trim only just settled, so airspeed sat near the 10 knot fast edge of the standard as the descent began. Nothing exceeded the tolerance, though the descent was started while the last trim change was still being made. SP is expected to configure 2 to 3 NM prior to the FAF so airspeed and trim are stable before the descent.

error_modes.label: Descent gradient not calculated for step-down fix restrictions inside the FAF

texts.0: SP, due to descent gradients never being calculated for the step-down fix restrictions inside the FAF, did not plan the descent against the published altitudes. The aircraft passed a step-down altitude more than 300 feet low with the rate unchanged, and the IP arrested the descent and regained the published profile. SP had not identified the step-down fixes during the approach briefing.
texts.1: SP, due to no gradient being computed from altitude to lose against distance available, arrived at the step-down fix about 300 feet above the planned profile, at the limit of the standard. The rate then flown to make the following restriction had to be corrected on IP call, and the remaining altitudes were met only with repeated prompts on rate and distance.
texts.2: SP, due to descent gradients estimated rather than calculated from altitude to lose and distance available, did not fly a rate that matched the step-down restrictions. The aircraft was about 230 feet high against the planned profile, between the 150 and 300 foot values of the standard, before SP increased the rate and made the restriction without IP input.
texts.3: SP calculated the descent gradient for the step-down fixes inside the FAF and flew a rate that met each published altitude. Profile error stayed within about 120 feet, inside the standard, and no restriction was approached from below. The rate required was briefed before the descent.
texts.4: SP computed the altitude to lose against the distance available for every step-down fix and flew each segment so the published altitude was reached at the fix with negligible error. Deviation from the planned profile stayed within a few tens of feet and no restriction was missed. The gradients were quoted during the approach briefing.
texts.marginal: SP met all step-down fix restrictions, but the rate was set from the altimeter alone rather than from a computed gradient, so the aircraft reached each fix close to the 150 foot edge of the planned profile. Every restriction was satisfied and none was penetrated. SP is expected to calculate the descent gradient for each step-down fix so the profile is flown rather than recovered.

error_modes.label: Flap setting and airspeed not adjusted for crosswind or gusty conditions

texts.0: SP, due to the final being flown at the standard configuration and speed in reported gusty conditions with none of the airspeed increase the technique allows, did not keep a working margin on the approach. The gusts drove the airspeed more than 10 knots below the approach speed with the aircraft in the full configuration, and the IP added power, adjusted the configuration and took the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to no allowance being made for the gust factor in the target approach speed, flew the final with the speed swinging on each gust. Airspeed reached about 10 knots below the approach speed, at the limit of the standard, and was contained only after the IP directed an increase in the target speed for the conditions.
texts.2: SP, due to the flap setting and target speed being left unadjusted for the crosswind and gusts, did not hold a stable speed on final. Airspeed dropped to about 8 knots below 110 KIAS, between the 5 and 10 knot values of the standard, before SP increased the target speed for the conditions and stabilized the approach without IP input.
texts.3: SP allowed for the gusty conditions with an increased target speed and the appropriate flap setting, and the airspeed stayed inside the standard through the gusts, no more than about 4 knots slow and 8 knots fast of the target. Power corrections remained small and the approach stayed stable to MDA.
texts.4: SP set the configuration and the target speed for the reported crosswind and gusts before the final and flew the approach with speed variations of about 3 knots despite the conditions. The gusts produced no divergence in speed or attitude and the aircraft was stable throughout the descent to MDA.
texts.marginal: SP made an allowance for the conditions, but the increase in target speed was smaller than the reported gust factor called for, so airspeed touched the 5 knot slow edge of the standard on the stronger gusts. The approach stayed inside the tolerance and was stable overall. SP is expected to size the speed increase to the reported gusts so the margin does not depend on the timing of a gust.
